Tuscarora Arboretum · Artifact No. 1

The 1937 Hamilton Bottle

Identification & History Guide

Martinsburg, West Virginia · October 2026

Identification & History Guide for a bottle patented in 1937 by the J. T. & A. Hamilton Company of Pittsburgh. The patent number — Des. 107,017, Serial No. 71,167, 1937 — documents a small bottle unearthed in the Irish Hill neighborhood, along the Tuscarora Creek, in Martinsburg, West Virginia, on October 25, 2026. The clear, small glass flask, marked by a patent on the bottom, is the design created by Lawrence J. Kihn in 1937 and granted to J. T. & A. Hamilton: a flat-oval druggist’s bottle with ribbed corner posts, made to be filled, paper-labeled, and sold from a drugstore shelf.

The Bottle, in Brief

A machine-made, unembossed druggist/toiletry stock bottle of the flat-oval panel family — small in the hand, at less than 4 inches tall, less than 3 inches wide, and about 1 inch thick, holding roughly 2–3 fluid ounces. It was made by the J. T. & A. Hamilton Company of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to the patented design of Lawrence J. Kihn of Pittsburgh. Bottles of this class were sold empty by the glasshouse and filled and paper-labeled by the druggist or small maker who retailed their contents. It most likely held a toilet preparation — hand or skin lotion, hair tonic, or toilet water — or a druggist’s own liquid preparation. (Contents: INFERENCE — from the bottle’s form, finish, and class.)

The raised embossing on the base reads “U.S. PAT. 107017” — U.S. Design Patent 107,017, “Design for a Glass Bottle,” filed August 18, 1937 and patented November 16, 1937 — and the patent’s drawing matches this bottle feature for feature: the flat front label panel, the corner posts ribbed with stacked horizontal ribs, the flat-oval “capsule” cross-section with notched corners, the narrow neck with a molded continuous screw thread, and the flat shoulder ledge. The bottle was therefore made in 1937 or later — late-1930s to 1940s production is most likely.

The bottle’s century on one line — tap a date to jump to its story.

⛏️ 1 · The Find — Irish Hill ↑ Timeline

On October 25, 2026, this bottle came out of the ground in Irish Hill, Martinsburg, West Virginia — the old neighborhood that slopes toward Tuscarora Creek. It came out intact, heavily crusted with the mineral skin that long burial writes on glass, and was gently cleaned: soft work, no harsh treatment. Clean, it is a squat flat-oval flask in nearly clear glass, with ribbed corner posts and a small threaded finish.

🔍 2 · The Bottle Up Close

FeatureWhat the bottle shows
Overall formA small, squat flat-oval flask. Glass manufacturers sold this silhouette to druggists for decades; the Society for Historical Archaeology (SHA) traces the flat-oval “Philadelphia Oval” through Illinois Glass Co. catalogs of 1903, 1908, and 1911 as a standard druggist shape. This ribbed-corner variant is Kihn’s patented 1937 design, made by Hamilton (§3).
Size & capacityLess than 4 inches tall, less than 3 inches wide, about 1 inch thick, with a narrow neck — a genuinely small bottle, at the small end of its class. A flat oval of those dimensions holds roughly 2–3 fluid ounces at most — an estimate computed from the dimensions.
Flat panels, front & backBroad flat faces made for a paper label, which carried the product’s name. No embossing anywhere on the body — the mark of generic stock ware, since national brands embossed their names into the glass.
Ribbed corner posts & shouldersThe four corner posts carry pronounced stacked horizontal ribs over their upper two-fifths, and similar ribbing wraps the shoulders — a dressed-up “gothic” treatment that made a cheap stock bottle presentable on a shelf, and the very feature Kihn’s patent drawing shows (§3).
Neck & finishThe neck is small and narrow, topped by a molded continuous screw thread (about two turns) above a smooth collar — the transfer bead the bottle machine gripped. Machine-made, and made for a standardized metal screw cap.
The glassNearly clear, with a faint lavender blush, strongest at the neck.
The baseA shallow recessed oval push-up carrying raised embossing that reads “U.S. PAT. 107017” — U.S. Design Patent 107,017, Lawrence J. Kihn’s “Design for a Glass Bottle,” assigned to the J. T. & A. Hamilton Company and patented November 16, 1937 (§3). No separate maker’s mark: the patent number is the attribution.
ConditionIntact, with the classic burial suite: iridescent weathering film, flaking patches, scratches, residual mineral staining (§9). Every trait matches long burial; nothing suggests a modern reproduction.

📜 3 · The Patent — Des. 107,017 ↑ Timeline

Some bottles carry their birth certificate on the bottom. The raised line in this bottle’s base — “U.S. PAT. 107017” — is the number of a United States design patent, and the document behind it names the designer, the maker, and the year the design entered the world.

The Patent — Full Record

Every particular below is taken from the patent document itself — the official document (drawing sheet and specification) as issued by the United States Patent Office.

FieldAs the document gives it
PatentU.S. Design Patent Des. 107,017
Title“Design for a Glass Bottle” (the drawing sheet is headed “Glass Bottle”)
InventorLawrence J. Kihn
Inventor’s residencePittsburgh, in the county of Allegheny and State of Pennsylvania — the specification states that Kihn was “a citizen of the United States, residing in Pittsburgh, in the county of Allegheny and State of Pennsylvania”
AssignorJ. T. & A. Hamilton Company, “a corporation of Pennsylvania”
Application filedAugust 18, 1937
Application Serial No.71,167
Patented (granted)November 16, 1937
Term of patent14 years
Attorneys (drawing sheet)Christy and Wharton — the drawing sheet is signed by the inventor and marked “By Christy and Wharton, Attorneys”
The claim, verbatim“I claim: The ornamental design for a glass bottle substantially as shown.”
The figures, as the patent describes them“In the drawing: Fig. I is a front elevation of a glass bottle showing my new design; Fig. II is a side elevation of the said glass bottle and Fig. III is a transverse sectional view in the plane indicated by the section line III–III in Fig. II.”

The drawing and the bottle

The patent drawing, compared against the cleaned bottle, point by point:

  • Flat front label panel — the broad flat face framed for a paper label in Fig. I is the bottle’s broad flat face.
  • Corner posts with stacked horizontal ribs on their upper portions — Fig. I stacks the ribs across the upper part of each corner post; the bottle’s four posts carry exactly that ribbing over their upper two-fifths (§2).
  • Flat-oval “capsule” cross-section with notched corners — Fig. III, the section taken on line III–III of Fig. II, is the bottle’s plan shape: a flattened oval whose corners step in where the posts stand.
  • Narrow neck with a molded continuous screw thread — drawn at the top of Fig. I and Fig. II; molded on the bottle, about two turns above the transfer-bead collar (§2).
  • Flat shoulder ledge — the level shelf where body meets neck in both elevations is the bottle’s shoulder.
  • Proportion — the drawing’s bottle is short, broad, and thin, as is the original: less than 4 inches tall, less than 3 inches wide, about 1 inch thick, roughly 2–3 fluid ounces (§2).

Five independent features, plus proportion — all present, none contradicted. A design patent protects how a thing looks. Hamilton registered this bottle’s look — the ribbed posts, the panel, the capsule section — and for fourteen years no rival house could copy it.

🗓️ 4 · The Date — 1937 and After ↑ Timeline

The floor. Kihn’s design was filed on August 18, 1937 and patented on November 16, 1937, so a bottle marked with its number was made in 1937 or later. The design’s 14-year term ran to 1951.

The likely window — INFERENCE. A new design is most heavily produced in the years right after its patenting, while the design is current and the term is young. Late-1930s–1940s production is the most likely window; production later in the term (to 1951) is not excluded.

The screw thread. By 1937, the molded continuous thread was simply how bottles were finished. Illinois Glass’s 1926 catalog had praised its screw finish as one that “has gained great favor among manufacturers of hair tonics and toilet waters” — a finish absent from its 1920 catalog — and toiletries led the finish’s adoption (SHA). Kihn drew a thread as a matter of course; it marks a machine-made bottle built for a standardized metal screw cap, its transfer-bead collar the machine’s grip mark.

The form. The flat-oval panel silhouette was catalog-standard druggist ware from the 1880s forward. Kihn’s 1937 design is that long-lived silhouette dressed for a new decade — ribbed posts, capsule section — a familiar shape given a protected, shelf-ready face.

🏭 5 · The Maker — J. T. & A. Hamilton Company, Pittsburgh ↑ Timeline

The bottle carries no separate maker’s mark — it does not need one. The base number is the attribution: the design was assigned, before patenting, to the J. T. & A. Hamilton Company, a corporation of Pennsylvania, of Pittsburgh — glass manufacturers, and the firm that produced bottles to this design. The designer of record is Lawrence J. Kihn of Pittsburgh, Allegheny County. Both names come from the patent document itself (§3).

Pittsburgh was one of America’s great glass cities — coal for the furnaces, sand in the hills, and rivers and railways to carry the ware away. A glasshouse there lived by the trade catalog and the gross: blank bottles by the hundreds of thousands, sold to druggists, manufacturers, and jobbers across the country. Hamilton’s 1937 patent shows the house at work in its era’s way — a Pittsburgh designer creates the form, assigns it to the company, and the company protects it for fourteen years before it ever reaches a mold.

Why this design, in 1937? Read the bottle as its decade wrote it. National Prohibition had been repealed in December 1933 — West Virginia followed in 1934 — and the legal drugstore trade in tonics, lotions, and toilet preparations was in full, crowded flower: tens of thousands of drugstores, shelves packed with competing preparations, every one of them needing a bottle. A stock blank could no longer afford to be invisible. So Hamilton’s blank wears its selling face in the glass itself: a broad panel waiting for a bright paper label, and corner posts ribbed like little columns — a “gothic” flourish that made a few cents’ worth of machine-made glass look considered, even handsome, on the shelf. The bottle is a reflection of its maker: Pittsburgh industry underneath — automatic machines, standardized caps, gross-lot economics — and retail salesmanship on the surface. (The reading of the design’s motive: INFERENCE from the form and its market.)

And the journey was ordinary, which is its own kind of evidence: glassware moved nationally by rail and jobber, and the B&O had linked Pittsburgh’s country and Martinsburg since the nineteenth century. A Pittsburgh bottle in a Martinsburg yard surprises no one who knows the trade. The factory is Pittsburgh; the shelf, in the end, was Irish Hill.

⚙️ 6 · Production & Circulation ↑ Timeline

By Hamilton’s production years the bottle industry was fully mechanized — by 1923, 94% of American bottles were already machine-made — and the numbers of that industry are documented. The first commercial Owens automatic machines (1905) produced nearly 13,000 bottles a day with two men, against some 3,500 a day from a seven-man hand crew, and cut the cost of a gross of bottles from $1.80 to 10–12 cents (University of Toledo / Owens-Illinois exhibit; ASME). The later AR machine reached 50,400 bottles a day.

13,000bottles a day from one Owens machine, 1905 — with a crew of two
94%of American bottles machine-made by 1923
144bottles to the gross — the unit of the stock-bottle trade

Stock druggist forms were sold by the gross — 144 at a time — out of catalogs like Illinois Glass’s 1906 catalog, which devotes spread after spread to “Druggist,” “Extracts & Panels,” and “Extract & Toilet” ware and sells the paper labels to go on them; its 1901 catalog prices druggists’ packing bottles explicitly “Per Gross.” From the glasshouse, bottles moved by rail and jobber to drugstores and small makers nationwide. No production total for this specific form or mold is documented — the industry figures describe the world it was made in, not a count of its twins.

🧴 7 · Purpose & Prevalence — How Widely Were These Used?

The flat-oval panel bottle was one of the default containers of the American drugstore age. The SHA’s toiletry research describes the class — perfume, cologne, lotions, hair products, Florida water — as smaller bottles, “rarely over about 10 or 12 ounces,” narrow-necked, thin-walled; the druggist shapes (French squares, Blakes, ovals) were “very frequently used by druggists for their products,” for prescriptions, patent medicines, and skin lotions alike. This bottle sits at the very small end of even that class range: at its measured size its capacity computes to roughly 2–3 fluid ounces (§2). The scale of the trade that consumed them is a matter of record:

  • 61,865 drug stores operated in the United States in 1929 — 57,812 of them independent (a 1929 Drug Topics census) — every one a customer for stock bottles by the gross.
  • The national market in pharmaceutical products grew from 2,700 items in 1880 to 38,000 by 1916 and 60,000 by 1933 — the shelf-filling explosion these blank bottles served.
  • Toilet preparations were a national mail-order category by 1908, when the Sears, Roebuck catalog carried hair tonic to farm and town alike.

For this bottle, the contents remain an inference, and it is labeled one: the combination of flat label panels, dressed-up ribbed corners, a narrow neck, and a standard screw cap best fits a toilet preparation — hand or skin lotion, hair tonic, or toilet water — the product class that had adopted screw caps earliest and kept them standard; a druggist’s own liniment, tonic, or prescription preparation is the second possibility; a national patent-medicine brand is unlikely, because those were embossed. (Contents: INFERENCE.) Period color: Hind’s Honey and Almond Cream — a comparable screw-top toilet preparation, sold from the 1910s into this bottle’s own decades — though the Hind’s bottles themselves are wider-necked and rectangular: relatives in product and price class, not form matches.

🏺 8 · Survival — How Many Remain?

The honest answer first: no census, registry, or count of surviving bottles of this class exists. Anyone who quotes a survival number for unembossed druggist bottles is inventing it. What the evidence does support:

  • The class survives abundantly. The collector forums where diggers report their finds are blunt about it: unembossed bottles are dug by the hundred from single dumps, and unembossed screw-top bottles “can be had by the thousands” in the woods behind any small town. Glass is nearly immortal in the ground; the discard stream of a 60,000-product drugstore age was enormous.
  • Museums hold them as assemblages, not counts. The Smithsonian’s patent-medicine collection preserves a whole Pennsylvania drugstore’s stock — 700-plus items — as a period document; individual druggist bottles sit in state collections as typology examples. No institution counts blank stock bottles by form.
  • This design is not traded under a collector’s name. With no face embossing, the bottle has no searchable trade name, and sellers cannot list what they cannot identify. What is genuinely scarce in this class is the paper label — the bottle survives; its product identity usually does not.

🌈 9 · What the Ground Wrote on It

The rainbow skin and staining are the bottle’s burial record, written by soil chemistry. Buried glass weathers by leaching: slightly acidic soil water draws the alkali out of the surface, leaving stacked, translucent, silica-rich layers a micron or less thick; light reflecting between those layers splits into iridescent colors — the same thin-film physics as an oil slick (Conservation Wiki/AIC; Corning Museum of Glass). The layers flake — the bottle’s peeling patches are delaminating lamellae — so the surface deserves the gentle handling it has had. Dissolved minerals precipitate as crust; sediment washes in through the mouth and cakes inside. One caution from the conservation literature: the old idea that iridescent layers accumulate one per year of burial “has since been discarded” (Brill 1961; Newton 1971) — the patina testifies to a long burial, never to a date. And a note on the color: much of what the unearthed photographs showed as deep color was this crust and staining; the cleaned glass keeps only its faint, true blush.

🗺️ 10 · West Virginia & Martinsburg — the Local Chapter

Glass country. By about 1910 the glass industry employed some 7,500 West Virginians — the state’s fourth-largest employer — and West Virginia accounted for an outsized share of the nation’s bottle production (West Virginia Encyclopedia). The raw material was local: high-purity Oriskany sandstone from Warm Springs Ridge in Morgan County, around Berkeley Springs, roughly 30 miles from Martinsburg, was quarried for glass sand from the Civil War era and became one of the world’s largest melting-sand operations. The automatic bottle machine itself was invented by Michael Owens of Point Pleasant, West Virginia; his company’s Fairmont plant (1910) ran around the clock at up to 180,000 bottles a day, with Clarksburg, Charleston, and Huntington plants following.

Made in Pittsburgh — and not in Martinsburg. The patent settles the factory (§5): the J. T. & A. Hamilton Company of Pittsburgh. No source documents a glass factory in Martinsburg or Berkeley County in the era; the county’s industry was textiles, brick, limestone, orchards, and distilling. This bottle almost certainly arrived by rail — the B&O reached Martinsburg in 1842. Its local itinerary is inference, the standard path for such ware and nothing more: filled or sold by a local druggist (period biographies record Arthur Merryman Gilbert as a Martinsburg druggist of over forty years), used up, and discarded on the Irish Hill ground where it was later found. (Local itinerary: INFERENCE.) No document records this bottle’s own journey.

After the dry years. National Prohibition was repealed in December 1933, and West Virginia’s voters repealed the state’s own dry law in 1934. A bottle made in 1937 or later belongs to the legal, labeled, post-repeal drugstore trade — the world of crowded shelves and competing brands that its ribbed, patent-protected face was designed for (§5).

Why it was in the ground — the likely deposition (INFERENCE). Households long buried refuse on their own lots — in privies, ash pits, and rear-lot trash pits — and the practice persisted well into the twentieth century, municipal collection or no. City archaeologists (Alexandria, Virginia) describe privies as “handy receptacles for the trash of daily life prior to regular garbage pickup,” often sealed when a family moved; National Park Service excavations of period privies recovered glass medicine bottles of the early twentieth century — this bottle’s class, from features that stayed in use for decades. Such pits stood in rear lots, behind the houses, where the outbuildings and service alleys were — in Irish Hill as in any Martinsburg neighborhood of the period. Which exact feature this bottle slept in, only its ground could say.

Martinsburg in a breath: laid out in the 1770s by General Adam Stephen along Tuscarora Creek — the creek this project is named for — and incorporated October 18, 1778; a B&O roundhouse town from 1842; its railroad destroyed in the Civil War (Jackson’s men hauled its locomotives away by horse team in 1861); and in 1877 the starting point of the Great Railroad Strike, America’s first nationwide industrial strike.

💵 11 · Value

Unembossed machine-era bottles sit at the common end of the bottle market: the diggers’ forums put realized values for the class at a few dollars; current asking prices for comparable unembossed utility bottles cluster at $15–$30 (asking, not sold); published guides place common machine-era bottles at $5–$20, with richer sun-purpled, labeled examples reaching higher bands this faint, unlabeled bottle does not fit. Weighing all of it:

General estimate: $10–$25 as a retail or decorative piece; $5–$15 the most likely realized price in an online sale.

Two notes. The base patent embossing adds no documented market premium: no listing, guide, or forum prices a bottle higher for a design-patent number on its base. Its premium is research value — this bottle’s story can be documented to a named designer, a named maker, and a dated drawing, which is more than most dug bottles ever get. And a buyer paying for that documented story — a photographed, researched artifact from Irish Hill, Martinsburg — might pay at or above the top of the range; that is a provenance premium with no comparable sale to pin a figure to, so none is claimed. (Provenance premium: ESTIMATE.)
